The Two Rivian Stories Investors Were Pricing In

The shares cost US$19.71 at the start of the period, and anyone looking at Rivian Automotive then had to choose between two very different but plausible scripts for the next few years.

On the bullish side, the earlier narrative put fair value at US$21.83. This was a price level implied by its assumptions rather than a stated fact, built on the idea that the R2 platform, in-house software and autonomy stack could drive margin improvements and new high-margin software revenue. The later, more cautious storyline saw fair value at US$14.04. This was again an implied price based on its own model, and still acknowledged that R2 and manufacturing efficiency might lower costs. Skeptics focused on risks around policy shifts, ongoing cash burn and the possibility that reliance on a narrow product line, especially R2, could leave Rivian exposed if midsize SUV demand or pricing turned out weaker than hoped.

Rivian Automotive securing Volkswagen’s 15.9% stake, a US$1b loan, and up to US$1.25b from Uber directly backed the bullish script that capital and partnerships would support the R2 platform and autonomy plans. At the same time, the business still reported a net loss of US$913m in Q3 2026, even though net margin improved to 42.4% from 75.3%. Overall, the evidence cut both ways.
